meta.blurb: On the last train of the winter, a rich man dies in his locked room, and everyone on board had a reason to hate him. Only a young guard and a sharp-eared old teacher notice that something is wrong. Can they solve it before the snow clears?
meta.bible: Ada Penrose: the youngest guard on the line, sharp-eyed, kind and brave; she works the night train. Mr Leopold Vane: the rich, hard owner of the Grand Harrow Hotel and half the town; dies on the train; takes five drops of heart medicine from a small blue bottle at ten every night. Felix Okoro: Vane's young secretary, honest but nervous. Mrs Imelda Crane: a widow who runs a café on the harbour; her husband Josiah lost his land to Vane twenty years ago. Josiah Crane: her late husband. Dr Hugh Alder: Vane's doctor and old friend, silver-haired and charming; the murderer. Captain Barnaby Frost: a retired lifeboat captain, loud but honest. Sandro Bellini: the cheerful steward of the dining car. Miss Agnes Birch: a retired schoolteacher with sharp ears and a knitting bag; she helps Ada. Carlow Junction: where the train starts. Harrow Bay: the seaside town at the end of the line. Gull Cutting: the gorge where the snow slide stops the train. Carriage C: the sleeping carriage with six rooms; Vane has the first room, Miss Birch the second. The Grand Harrow Hotel: Vane's hotel. The train: the last one before the line closes for the winter; leaves at nine o'clock and is due at Harrow Bay in the morning. Voice and tone: cosy, clever and warm, a fair-play puzzle told step by step; the death is stated plainly and without gore; the clues are the half-empty bottle that is full at eleven, the clink of glass at twenty to ten, and the doctor's lie.

beats.scene: A young guard with a lamp checks tickets on a snowy night platform
beats.summary: Ada Penrose, the youngest guard, begins her shift on the last train of the winter from Carlow Junction to Harrow Bay.

beats.scene: A rich old man boards the train, followed by his secretary with a leather case
beats.summary: Mr Vane, the rich owner of the Grand Harrow Hotel, boards with his secretary Felix Okoro and takes the first room in Carriage C.

beats.scene: A grey-haired woman in a plain coat stops short when she sees Mr Vane
beats.summary: Mrs Crane, a harbour widow, boards with a letter in her hand and goes pale at the sight of Vane.

beats.scene: A silver-haired doctor and an old sea captain climb aboard together
beats.summary: Dr Alder, Vane's own doctor, and Captain Frost, a retired lifeboat captain who glares at Vane, board the train.

beats.scene: A tiny old lady with a huge knitting bag offers the guard a peppermint
beats.summary: Miss Agnes Birch, a retired schoolteacher with sharp ears, boards last and gives Ada a peppermint.

beats.scene: The night train pulls out of the snowy station into the dark
beats.summary: The train leaves at nine o'clock along the cliff line, due at Harrow Bay by morning.

beats.scene: A steward in a white jacket shows the guard a cream-coloured letter
beats.summary: Bellini the steward tells Ada that every passenger in Carriage C received the same letter from Vane inviting them on this train.

beats.scene: A pale secretary leaves a lamp-lit room while a brass key swings on a chain
beats.summary: At a quarter past nine Okoro delivers papers to Vane and comes out pale; Vane's leather case is locked with a small brass key on his watch chain.

beats.scene: Mr Vane holds a small blue bottle up to the lamp in his room
beats.summary: Vane tells Ada that he takes five drops of heart medicine at ten every night, and the blue bottle is half empty.

beats.scene: Mrs Crane and Mr Vane argue behind a door while Ada waits in the corridor
beats.summary: At twenty-five past nine Mrs Crane quarrels with Vane about twenty years of debt and leaves in tears.

beats.scene: Mr Vane walks down the corridor with a towel while the doctor stays inside
beats.summary: At half past nine Dr Alder goes in to examine Vane; a few minutes later Vane goes to the washroom with a towel, leaving the doctor alone in the room.

beats.scene: The doctor steps out as the steward brings a cup of cocoa on a tray
beats.summary: Vane returns, Dr Alder leaves with a good night, and Bellini brings Vane a cup of cocoa.

beats.scene: Captain Frost shakes a finger at Mr Vane in the narrow corridor
beats.summary: At ten to ten Captain Frost angrily accuses Vane of tearing down the old lifeboat house, until Bellini calms them.

beats.scene: Mr Vane says good night at his door while Ada listens to the lock
beats.summary: At ten o'clock Vane says good night and locks his compartment door from inside.

beats.scene: Two men play draughts in the lamp-lit dining car while another writes a letter
beats.summary: Dr Alder and Captain Frost play draughts and Okoro writes a letter in the dining car while Mrs Crane and Miss Birch stay in their rooms.

beats.scene: A great wall of snow and rock blocks the track in front of the stopped train
beats.summary: At twenty to eleven the train stops in Gull Cutting, where a slide of snow and rock has buried the line and the telegraph wire.

beats.scene: Passengers in coats and blankets crowd into the dining car, worried and cold
beats.summary: Ada tells the passengers that the train must wait until morning, and they gather in the dining car, all except Vane.

beats.scene: Ada unlocks Mr Vane's door with a long key and stares inside
beats.summary: At eleven Ada unlocks Vane's door with her master key and finds him dead in his chair.

beats.scene: Dr Alder kneels beside the still man and shakes his head gravely
beats.summary: Dr Alder examines Vane briefly and declares that he died of heart failure.

beats.scene: Ada looks closely at a blue bottle standing full beside the lamp
beats.summary: Ada notices that the blue bottle, half empty at nine, is now full to the neck, and the medicine smells sharp and bitter.

beats.scene: Ada whispers to Miss Birch in the corridor outside the dead man's room
beats.summary: Ada quietly tells Miss Birch about the bottle, and the old teacher says she heard something odd that evening.

beats.scene: Miss Birch points at the thin wall between her room and Vane's
beats.summary: Miss Birch heard glass clink and a cork squeak in Vane's room at twenty to ten, when Vane was in the washroom.

beats.scene: Ada tries a silent telegraph set in the guard's van by lamplight
beats.summary: The telegraph wire is down, so no help can come until morning and Ada decides to find the truth herself.

beats.scene: Felix Okoro answers questions nervously in the lamp-lit dining car
beats.summary: Okoro says he left papers with Vane at a quarter past nine and then wrote a letter, but will not say to whom.

beats.scene: Mrs Crane sits very straight with a folded letter in her lap
beats.summary: Mrs Crane admits she hated Vane, who took her husband's harbour land twenty years ago with a paper her husband never signed.

beats.scene: Captain Frost folds his thick arms while he is questioned at a dining table
beats.summary: Captain Frost says openly that he hated Vane for the lifeboat house, but that he sat playing draughts with Dr Alder from five to ten.

beats.scene: Bellini wrings a white cloth between his hands behind the dining car counter
beats.summary: Bellini describes making the cocoa and admits that Vane dismissed him from the hotel kitchens, but swears he is innocent.

beats.scene: Dr Alder sits with folded hands and answers Ada's questions with a smile
beats.summary: Dr Alder says he examined Vane at half past nine, left at once and went to his own room, and never touched anything; Ada knows this is not true.

beats.scene: Ada and Miss Birch open a leather case with a small brass key
beats.summary: Ada takes the brass key from Vane's watch chain, opens the leather case, and finds an old deed and a letter to Mrs Crane.

beats.scene: Ada reads an old man's letter aloud beside an oil lamp
beats.summary: Vane's letter confesses that he forged a deed twenty years ago, promises to return the true deed, and says he will name the friend who helped him.

beats.scene: Mrs Crane weeps over the letter while Ada watches kindly
beats.summary: Mrs Crane reads the letter and weeps; she had no reason to kill a man who was about to give back what she had lost.

beats.scene: Okoro and Captain Frost stand side by side, looking relieved and uneasy
beats.summary: Okoro admits he knew about Vane's plan and had been writing to a lawyer; Ada believes him and the captain.

beats.scene: Ada sits at a small corridor desk, looking along a row of closed doors
beats.summary: From her desk Ada could see every door; between twenty to ten and a quarter to ten only the doctor was in Vane's room.

beats.scene: Ada and Miss Birch count the clues on their fingers in the dim corridor
beats.summary: Ada and Miss Birch put together the clues: the half-empty bottle, the clink of glass, the doctor alone in the room, and his lie.

beats.scene: Ada politely asks the doctor to open his black bag in the dining car
beats.summary: Ada asks to look inside Dr Alder's bag; he hands it over calmly, though his knuckles are white.

beats.scene: Ada lifts a small glass bottle with a dropper from under a roll of bandages
beats.summary: Ada finds a nearly empty glass bottle with a dropper, labelled with a warning, that smells like the medicine in Vane's room.

beats.scene: Dr Alder shrugs while Ada holds the little bottle up in the lamplight
beats.summary: Dr Alder says that every doctor carries such drops, but Ada shows that the dropper is still damp and the smell matches.

beats.scene: Mrs Crane holds an old folded paper in a shaking hand
beats.summary: Mrs Crane produces the forged deed she has kept for twenty years, with Hugh Alder's name as witness.

beats.scene: Ada faces the doctor in the dining car while everyone watches in silence
beats.summary: Ada lays out the whole chain of clues before everyone: the bottle, the clink, the lie and the motive.

beats.scene: Dr Alder grips the edge of a table, no longer smiling
beats.summary: Dr Alder protests, but Miss Birch describes the clink of glass and the cork, and his hands begin to shake.

beats.scene: Dr Alder speaks quietly, looking at the floor, while no one moves
beats.summary: Dr Alder confesses that Vane planned to expose him, and that he topped up Vane's bottle with strong drops while Vane was at the washroom.

beats.scene: Dr Alder sits weary and old as he speaks to the silent passengers
beats.summary: Alder says he knew Vane would take his five drops at ten and that a doctor's word on a patient's death would never be questioned.

beats.scene: Two men guard a closed compartment door with the doctor sitting inside
beats.summary: Ada asks Captain Frost and Okoro to guard the doctor in an empty compartment until the police arrive.

beats.scene: Ada sits beside Mrs Crane with a blanket and a hot cup of tea
beats.summary: In the small hours Ada sits with Mrs Crane, who reads Vane's letter again, while Miss Birch passes round peppermints.

beats.scene: A bright winter dawn shows workers shovelling snow from the railway line
beats.summary: At first light a work crew from Harrow Bay clears the slide and the train moves on.

beats.scene: Police wait on the platform at Harrow Bay as the train glides in
beats.summary: At Harrow Bay Ada hands the police the bottle, the vial and the letter, and Dr Alder is led away.

beats.scene: Mrs Crane holds the true deed in her hands beside the harbour wall
beats.summary: Okoro helps Mrs Crane claim the true deed; the harbour land returns to the fishing families and the lifeboat house is to be rebuilt.

beats.summary: By spring Mrs Crane's café is busy, the lifeboat bell rings again, and Okoro works for an honest lawyer.

beats.scene: Miss Birch pats Ada's hand and gives her a peppermint on the platform
beats.summary: Miss Birch praises Ada, and the railway offers her a desk job, but Ada prefers to stay a guard.

beats.scene: Ada waves her lantern at the carriage door as a spring train rolls out
beats.summary: When the railway reopens in spring, Ada is back at the carriage door with her lamp, noticing everything.

B1B2: Ada Penrose, the youngest guard on the line, walks along the snowy platform at Carlow Junction with her lamp. Tonight is the last train before the little railway closes for the winter, and she wants everything to go well.
Mr Leopold Vane, who owns the Grand Harrow Hotel and half of the town, takes the first sleeping room in Carriage C. His young secretary, Felix Okoro, follows him carrying a heavy leather case.
Mrs Imelda Crane, a widow who runs a small café by the harbour, climbs aboard with a letter in her hand. When she sees Mr Vane through the open door of his room, she stops and turns pale.
Dr Hugh Alder, Mr Vane's own doctor, carries a black bag aboard. Behind him comes old Captain Barnaby Frost, who once led the Harrow Bay lifeboat, and he glares at Mr Vane's door.
The last passenger is Miss Agnes Birch, a retired schoolteacher with a huge knitting bag and very sharp ears. She gives Ada a peppermint and says that she never sleeps well on trains.
At nine o'clock exactly the train pulls out of Carlow Junction and heads north along the coast. Ada knows that the line runs high above the sea, and that it will not reach Harrow Bay until morning.
Sandro Bellini, the steward, tells Ada that every passenger in Carriage C has received a letter from Mr Vane. Each of them was asked to travel on this train tonight, and nobody will say why.

At a quarter past nine, Felix Okoro takes some papers to Mr Vane's room and comes out looking pale. Ada notices that the leather case on the table is locked with a small brass key on Vane's watch chain.
Mr Vane tells Ada that he must take five drops of his heart medicine every night at ten. He holds the little blue bottle up to the lamp, and she sees that it is only half full.
At twenty-five past nine Mrs Crane goes into Mr Vane's room and shuts the door. Ada hears angry voices and the words twenty years, and soon the widow comes out in tears.
At half past nine, Dr Alder goes in to check Mr Vane's heart. A few minutes later Vane walks past Ada with a towel on his way to wash, while the doctor stays behind in the room.
Mr Vane comes back from the washroom, and Dr Alder leaves with a polite good night. Soon afterwards Sandro Bellini brings a cup of cocoa, and Vane drinks half of it.
At ten to ten, Captain Frost stops Mr Vane in the corridor and shakes a finger at him. He says that Vane tore down the old lifeboat house, and the steward has to calm them down.
At ten o'clock Mr Vane says good night to Ada and locks his door from the inside. She hears the click clearly, and Miss Birch, in the next room, hears it too.
In the dining car, Dr Alder and Captain Frost play draughts without speaking, while Mr Okoro writes a letter at the next table. Mrs Crane stays in her room, and Miss Birch sits in hers, knitting.
At twenty to eleven the train slows with a long, shuddering scream of brakes and stops in Gull Cutting. Ada goes out with her lantern and finds a great slide of snow and rock across the line.
Ada tells the passengers that nobody can leave the train until morning. They gather in the dining car in their coats, and everyone is there except Mr Vane, who is sleeping behind his locked door.
At eleven Ada knocks on Mr Vane's door, but there is no answer. She unlocks it with her master key and finds him sitting in his armchair, quite still and cold.
Ada fetches Dr Alder, who kneels by the old man and examines him for a minute. He says that it is plainly heart failure, and that he often warned Vane about his weak heart.
While the doctor talks, Ada looks around the room and sees the little blue bottle by the lamp. It is full to the neck, and she remembers that it was only half full at a quarter past nine.
In the corridor, Ada quietly tells Miss Birch about the bottle. The old teacher listens with her head on one side, and says that she heard something strange that evening.
Miss Birch tells Ada that at twenty to ten she heard the clink of glass through the thin wall. Mr Vane's slippers had just passed her door on the way to the washroom, so someone else was in his room.
Ada tries to send a message, but the telegraph wire is down under the snow. There will be no police and no help until morning, so she decides to find out the truth herself.

Ada questions each passenger in the dining car. Felix Okoro says that he left papers with Mr Vane at a quarter past nine, saw nothing strange, and spent the evening writing, but his hands shake as he speaks.
Mrs Crane admits that Mr Vane's letter invited her on this train, and that she hates him for the harbour land he took from her husband. After their quarrel, she says, she cried alone in her room.

Captain Frost says openly that he hated Mr Vane for pulling down the old lifeboat house. He insists that he went to the dining car at five to ten and played draughts with Dr Alder until Ada called them.

Sandro Bellini explains that he made the cocoa himself and carried it to Mr Vane at a quarter to ten. He admits that Vane dismissed him from the hotel kitchens last month, but he says that he would never harm anyone.
Dr Alder says that he examined Mr Vane at half past nine and found his heart steady. He says that he said good night at once and went to his own room, and that he never touched anything on the table.
Ada and Miss Birch go back into Mr Vane's room together. They take the brass key from his watch chain, open the leather case, and find an old deed with a red seal and a letter.

In the letter, Mr Vane confesses that twenty years ago he used a false paper to take Josiah Crane's land. He writes that he will give back the true deed in the morning and name the friend who helped him.
Mrs Crane reads the letter and cries quietly. She says that she never knew Mr Vane meant to put things right, so she had no reason at all to wish him dead.
Okoro admits that Mr Vane told him about the plan, and that he was writing to a lawyer for advice. He was afraid that a poor secretary would be blamed, and Ada believes him.
Ada sits at her little desk in the corridor and thinks back over the evening. She could see every door, and between twenty to ten and a quarter to ten nobody entered Mr Vane's room.
Ada and Miss Birch count the facts together: the half-empty bottle, the clink of glass, and the doctor alone in the room. Only one man fits, and he told Ada a lie about it.
In front of the other passengers, Ada asks Dr Alder politely if she may look inside his black bag. He smiles and says that he has nothing to hide, but his hand tightens on the handle.
Under the bandages, Ada finds a small glass bottle with a dropper. It is nearly empty, it smells sharp and bitter like the blue bottle, and its label says one drop only.
Dr Alder shrugs and says that every doctor carries strong drops like these. Ada answers that the dropper is still damp, so it has been used tonight.
Mrs Crane takes an old paper from her bag and says that she has kept it for twenty years. It is the false deed that ruined her husband, and under it is the witness's name, Hugh Alder.
Ada lays out the whole chain of clues in front of everyone. The doctor was alone in the room at twenty to ten, he lied about it, and he had a reason to fear Mr Vane's confession.
Dr Alder says that it is all nonsense, and that a guard cannot accuse a doctor. But when Miss Birch repeats the sound of the glass and the cork, his hands begin to shake.
At last Dr Alder tells the truth. Mr Vane had planned to confess everything at breakfast, and the doctor knew that his name, his work and his freedom would all be lost.
Dr Alder says that he knew Vane would take his five drops at ten. He had counted on a quiet death that everyone would blame on a weak heart, and on being the first to examine the body.
Ada asks Okoro and Captain Frost to guard the doctor in an empty compartment. The doctor goes quietly, and the other passengers settle down to wait for morning.
Ada sits with Mrs Crane while the snow falls outside, and the widow reads Mr Vane's letter again. Miss Birch passes round peppermints, and the carriage slowly grows quiet.
At dawn a work crew arrives from Harrow Bay with shovels and a small engine. Within a few hours the line is clear, and the train begins the last slow part of its journey.
At Harrow Bay the police are waiting on the platform in the morning light. Ada hands over the blue bottle, the little vial and Mr Vane's letter, and the doctor is led away quietly.
The true deed is given to Mrs Crane, and Felix Okoro helps her with the lawyers. The harbour land goes back to the fishing families, and the old lifeboat house will be built again.
By spring Mrs Crane's café is busy again beside the harbour, and Captain Frost rings the bell of the new lifeboat house. Okoro works for an honest lawyer, and the town feels lighter.
On the platform, Miss Birch shakes Ada's hand and says that she has the sharpest eyes on the line. The railway company offers her a desk job, but Ada says that she likes walking the carriages.
When the little railway opens again in spring, the first train leaves Carlow Junction in bright sunshine. Ada stands at the carriage door with her lamp, ready for whatever the journey brings.
C1C2: Snow was falling softly over Carlow Junction as Ada Penrose, the youngest guard on the whole line, walked down the platform with her lamp and her ticket book. Tonight's train to Harrow Bay was the last one before the little railway closed for the winter, and she was determined that nothing should spoil it. She had no idea that before dawn she would be the only person on board who believed that a death had not been an accident.

Leopold Vane, the owner of the Grand Harrow Hotel and, it was said, of half the town besides, swept aboard as though the train had been built for him alone. His young secretary, Felix Okoro, trailed behind, clutching a heavy leather case that Vane never allowed anyone else to carry. The old man took the first sleeping room in Carriage C, and he did not trouble to thank the guard who held the door.

Imelda Crane, a plain-spoken widow who kept a small café on the harbour at Harrow Bay, climbed aboard clutching a folded letter as though it might fly out of her hand. Glancing along the corridor, she caught sight of Vane through the door of his room, and the colour drained from her weathered face. Ada, who noticed most things, wondered what could make a woman look at a rich man with such old and quiet anger.

Dr Hugh Alder, a smooth, silver-haired physician who had looked after Vane's heart for twenty years, stepped aboard with his black bag and a courteous word for the guard. Behind him came Captain Barnaby Frost, a retired lifeboat captain with a face like weathered rope, who stared at Vane's door as if he would gladly have pulled it from its hinges. The corridor, Ada thought, was beginning to feel crowded with old grudges.

The last passenger to board was Miss Agnes Birch, a retired schoolteacher no taller than a child, who carried a vast knitting bag and wore the keen, patient expression of someone who had spent forty years detecting whispers in the back row. She pressed a peppermint into Ada's hand and confided that she never slept on trains, so the guard would find her awake whenever she was wanted. Ada thanked her, little guessing how soon those sharp ears would be needed.

At nine o'clock exactly the whistle shrieked, the carriages jerked, and the night train pulled out of Carlow Junction into a darkness thick with snow. The line to Harrow Bay clung to the cliffs for most of its length, and Ada knew every bend of it, every tunnel and every weak spot where winter storms liked to bring down the rocks. Carriage C, with its six sleeping rooms, held the only passengers she was likely to see before morning.

Sandro Bellini, the cheerful steward from the dining car, whispered to Ada that every passenger in Carriage C had received the very same cream-coloured letter from Mr Vane. Each of them had been invited, in the old man's firm handwriting, to travel on this particular train, and none of them seemed willing to say what the letter had promised. Ada, who liked tidy explanations, felt the first faint prickle of unease.

At a quarter past nine, Felix Okoro carried a bundle of papers into Vane's room and came out a few minutes later looking pale and thoughtful, like a man who has just heard unexpected news. Through the half-open door Ada glimpsed the old leather case on the table, locked with a small brass key that Vane wore on his watch chain. She thought no more about it, though later she would wish that she had looked harder.

Vane, who enjoyed complaining to anyone in earshot, informed Ada that he took five drops of his heart medicine at ten o'clock every night, and that he would not miss them for a kingdom. He held the little blue bottle up to the lamp so that she could see how little remained, and she noticed that the liquid stood only halfway up the glass. It seemed an unimportant detail at the time, which is exactly why she remembered it.

At twenty-five past nine Imelda Crane knocked at Vane's door and went in, and for several minutes the thin walls of Carriage C carried the sound of two voices raised in anger. Ada caught only the words twenty years and you owe me before the widow came out with her chin high and her eyes full of tears. She walked straight to her own room and closed the door without a word to anyone.

At half past nine Dr Alder went in to examine his old patient, as he did every evening, and a few minutes later Vane strode past Ada's little desk with a towel over his arm, bound for the washroom at the end of the carriage. The doctor, he announced over his shoulder, might stay and write his notes in comfort, since the compartment had the better lamp. Ada heard the door close behind him and thought nothing of it.

When Vane returned from the washroom, the doctor was just stepping out of the compartment, smiling and saying that all was well with his heart. A few minutes later Bellini arrived with a steaming cup of cocoa on a tray, and Ada watched the old man drink half of it with evident satisfaction. Nothing in his manner suggested that he had little more than half an hour to live.

At ten minutes to ten Captain Frost, a man not used to hiding his feelings, planted himself in the corridor and accused Vane of tearing down the old lifeboat house to make room for a hotel garden. His voice shook the windows, and for a moment Ada thought the old sailor might strike the old landlord, but Bellini stepped between them with a soothing word. Vane only laughed a dry little laugh and said that by tomorrow everyone would see that he was not the man they thought.

As the clock in the corridor struck ten, Vane wished Ada a curt good night, stepped into his compartment and locked the door from the inside with a firm click that she and Miss Birch, in the next room, both heard. It was his nightly habit, he had told her, never to leave a door unlocked on a train. Down the corridor the other passengers drifted toward the dining car, as people do when sleep is still a long way off.

In the dining car the lamps glowed warmly on polished wood, and Dr Alder and Captain Frost sat down to a silent game of draughts as though nothing at all had happened. Felix Okoro scribbled a long letter at the next table, glancing up whenever the door opened, while Mrs Crane kept to her room and Miss Birch sat knitting in hers. Ada made her slow rounds of the carriage, listening to the steady drumming of the wheels.

At twenty to eleven the brakes shrieked, the carriages shuddered, and the train stopped dead in the narrow gorge known as Gull Cutting, with the sea booming somewhere far below. Ada climbed down with her lantern and found that a great slide of snow, earth and broken rock had buried the track ahead, and that the telegraph wire lay snapped beneath it. No help could reach them until a work crew came from Harrow Bay in the morning.

Ada gathered the passengers in the dining car and explained, as calmly as she could, that the train would stay where it was until morning and that no one could safely leave it. Dr Alder made light of the delay, Captain Frost grumbled about the cold, and Mrs Crane sat silent with her eyes on the black window, but nobody thought of waking Vane. It was only when the clock showed eleven that Ada remembered her rounds.

At eleven o'clock Ada knocked at Vane's door to make sure that he was warm enough, and when no answer came she grew uneasy and unlocked it with her master key. The compartment was bright and silent, the lamp still burning, and Leopold Vane sat in his armchair with his head fallen to one side, as pale and still as marble. Even before she touched his wrist she knew that he was dead.

Ada sent for Dr Alder, who came at once, knelt beside the body with a grave expression and, after a very brief examination, pronounced that death had come from heart failure. He had warned poor Vane a hundred times, he sighed, that the strain of business would kill him, and he suggested that the body be covered and left in peace until morning. His haste to close the matter seemed to Ada a little unusual in a man who had just lost an old friend.

While the doctor spoke, Ada's eyes travelled around the compartment, noting the shut window, the half-drunk cocoa and the little blue bottle standing beside the lamp with its cork pushed firmly home. Then she frowned, for the bottle she had seen held up to this very lamp barely two hours earlier had been half empty, and now the medicine stood almost to the top of the glass. A bottle may be emptied by use, she reflected, but it cannot fill itself.

Ada slipped out into the corridor, where Miss Birch was waiting in her dressing gown with her knitting still in her hands, and quietly described the bottle that had somehow filled itself. The old schoolteacher listened with her head on one side, like a thrush listening for a worm, and said that she had heard something odd that evening and had not known what to make of it. Ada understood at once that she had found an ally.

Miss Birch explained that at twenty to ten she had heard a small, sharp clink of glass through the thin wall between her room and Vane's, followed by the faint squeak of a cork being pressed home. She was quite sure of the time because she had heard Vane's heavy slippers go by her door a moment before, which meant that the old man himself had been in the washroom. Somebody, therefore, had been alone in his compartment with that bottle.

Ada tried the little telegraph set in the guard's van, but the wire was dead, buried beneath tons of snow, and the nearest signal box was miles away. With no police within reach and a train full of people who might each have had a reason to wish Vane dead, she realised that the questions would have to be hers. Miss Birch, who did not need to be asked twice, offered to keep her ears open.

One by one, Ada called her passengers to a corner of the dining car and asked them to account for their evening, beginning with Felix Okoro, whose hands trembled on the tablecloth. He had left the papers with Vane at a quarter past nine, he said, noticed nothing unusual and spent the rest of the evening writing in the dining car, though he refused to say to whom the letter was addressed. Ada made a note of that refusal and moved on.

Imelda Crane sat very straight, her folded letter in her lap, and admitted without flinching that Vane had invited her aboard and that she had gone to his room to tell him exactly what she thought of him. Twenty years earlier, she said, he had taken her husband's land beside the harbour with a paper that Josiah Crane had sworn he never signed, and Josiah had died poor and heartbroken. After the quarrel she had wept alone in her room until the train stopped, and she could produce no witness to say so.

Captain Frost folded his thick arms and declared, in a voice that made the glasses rattle, that he had hated Vane for ten years because the old man had torn down the lifeboat house where his crews had trained. He had never raised a hand against him, however, and from five minutes to ten until Ada called them he had sat over a game of draughts with Dr Alder, as the steward could prove. Ada found, to her surprise, that she believed him.

Sandro Bellini wrung a white cloth between his hands as he described how he had prepared the cocoa himself, carried it straight to Vane's compartment and watched the old man drink half of it. He confessed, rather unhappily, that Vane had dismissed him from the hotel kitchens only a month before, which gave him a reason to resent his late employer, but he swore that he had never wished anyone harm. Ada set the half-empty cup aside for the police to test, though she did not think that the cocoa was the answer.

Dr Alder answered with perfect calm, folding his long white hands, that he had listened to Vane's heart at half past nine and found it as steady as it had been for years. He had said good night at once, he claimed, retired to his own room to write his notes and joined Captain Frost at five minutes to ten, and he had certainly never touched anything in Vane's compartment. Ada thanked him politely, and said nothing about what she had seen from her desk in the corridor.

Returning to the compartment with Miss Birch, Ada took the small brass key from the dead man's watch chain and opened the leather case that he had guarded so jealously. Inside lay an old, yellowed deed with a heavy red seal, and beneath it a long letter in Vane's firm handwriting, addressed to Mrs Imelda Crane. Ada hesitated only a moment before she unfolded it, for a death had made the rules of politeness look very small.

The letter was a confession, and a bitter one: twenty years earlier, Vane wrote, he had forged a deed to seize Josiah Crane's land beside the harbour, and he had lived with the shame ever since. He had decided at last to hand the true deed back to Josiah's widow in the morning, and to tell the whole town about the friend who had put his name to the false paper, since such a witness must share the blame. Ada read the final lines twice, and a cold idea began to form in her mind.

When Ada gave her the letter, Imelda Crane read it through twice with her lips pressed together, and then, to everyone's surprise, she wept. She had come on the train, she said, expecting only a cold refusal, and she could never have wished Vane dead when he had been about to give back everything that she had lost. Ada believed her tears, and she quietly crossed the widow's name from her list.

Okoro finally confessed that Vane had told him of the plan to return the deed, and that he had spent the evening writing to a lawyer in Harrow Bay for help, fearing that a poor secretary would be blamed for any mischief. His honest embarrassment convinced Ada, and the steward's account of the game of draughts left Captain Frost without a speck of suspicion. That left only the bottle, and the question of who had stood alone in the room with it.

Ada sat down at her little desk in the corridor, from which she had watched the doors of all six rooms through the whole evening, and went over the minutes in her mind. Between twenty to ten and a quarter to ten, while Vane was at the washroom, no one had entered or left his compartment except the single man who had been left inside with the lamp, the bottle and the table. And that man had told her, with a charming smile, that he had said good night at once and gone to his own room.

Miss Birch counted the facts off on her knitting needles, as though she were reciting a lesson: the half-empty bottle at nine, the clink of glass at twenty to ten, the door that closed behind the doctor, and the full bottle at eleven. Ada added the final point, that Dr Alder had lied about leaving at once, and neither of them could find another explanation. The doctor who had been so quick to sign for a natural death was the one man who had both the chance and, perhaps, a reason.

In front of the other passengers, Ada asked Dr Alder, very politely, whether she might look inside his black medical bag, since it was the only bag on the train that carried medicines. He smiled and said that he had nothing to hide, and he handed it over with every appearance of calm, though Miss Birch noticed that his knuckles had gone white around the handle before he let go. Ada opened the clasp and began to lift out bandages, one by one.

Beneath the bandages lay a small glass bottle with a dropper and a faded label that said, in a doctor's neat writing, one drop only. It was almost empty, and when Ada drew out the stopper she smelled the same sharp, bitter odour that had hung over the blue bottle in Vane's compartment. The passengers watched in silence, and somewhere outside a gust of wind threw snow against the windows.

The doctor shrugged elegantly and remarked that every physician carries strong drops of the kind, and that Ada had found nothing more sinister than a tool of his trade. Ada held the little dropper up to the lamp and pointed out that it was still damp, that the bottle was nearly empty, and that the smell was exactly the one that hung over the blue bottle in Vane's room. For the first time that evening, Dr Alder did not smile.

Then Imelda Crane rose from her seat with an old, brown, folded paper in her hand, which she said she had carried everywhere for twenty years in the hope that someone would one day explain it. It was the forged copy of the deed that had ruined her husband, and at the bottom, beneath the false signature of Josiah Crane, stood the witness's name in a neat, careful hand: Hugh Alder, surgeon. A murmur ran around the dining car like a wind through reeds.

Standing in the flickering lamplight, Ada laid out the whole story for the passengers to hear: the half-empty bottle, the clink of glass, the doctor who had stayed behind in the room and then lied about it, and the confession that would have exposed his name at dawn. She did not raise her voice, for she did not need to, and the silence in the dining car grew heavier with every point. Dr Alder, still seated, listened as one might listen to a story about a stranger.

Dr Alder at last rose and protested that this was nonsense, that a young guard had no right to accuse a physician of lifelong good standing, and that the police would laugh at her in the morning. Miss Birch, however, calmly described the clink of glass and the squeak of the cork that she had heard through the wall, and she named the very minute with a teacher's confidence. He sat down again slowly, and for the first time his long white hands began to tremble.

At last the doctor spoke, quietly and without his usual charm, and told them that Vane had informed him at half past nine of his plan to confess everything at breakfast, naming every person who had helped him twenty years before. Alder had been young and poor then, he said, and had signed as witness for a gift of money, and the thought of losing his name, his patients and his freedom in his old age had been more than he could bear. While Vane was at the washroom, he had filled the blue bottle to the neck from a vial of his own strong drops.

He had known, he said, that Vane would take his five drops at ten o'clock as he always did, and that a dose from a bottle mixed so strongly would stop a heart without leaving any mark to show how. He had counted on being the first to examine the body and the last to be questioned, since no one doubts a doctor's word on the death of his own patient. His plan, he admitted, had failed only because a young guard had noticed a bottle that was too full.

Ada, who had no powers of arrest but a great deal of common sense, asked Captain Frost and Felix Okoro to stand guard over the doctor in an empty compartment until the police arrived. Alder walked there quietly, like a man who has stopped fighting, and the door was locked behind him with the guard's own master key. In the dining car the passengers, drained and silent, settled down to wait out the long night.

In the small hours Ada wrapped a blanket around the shivering widow and brought her a cup of tea, and the two women sat side by side while the snow fell silently against the windows. Mrs Crane read Vane's last letter once more, and murmured that it was strange to be given back, by a dead man's hand, the thing that a living one had stolen. Miss Birch passed round her peppermints, and one by one the weary passengers slipped into uneasy sleep.

At first light a work crew arrived from Harrow Bay with shovels, lanterns and a small clanking engine, and by nine o'clock the great slide had been cleared away from the track. Ada, who had not slept at all, walked beside the line in the clean, cold air and felt proud, and a little frightened, that so much had been decided in the course of a single night. The train gave a long whistle and crept forward under a sky as pale and bright as milk.

The police were waiting on the platform at Harrow Bay when the train pulled in, for word of the delay had reached them by another route. Ada handed the inspector the blue bottle, the glass dropper and Vane's letter, and described the long night in clear, careful order, while Dr Alder was led quietly away between two constables. He did not look back, and nobody on the platform spoke until the door of the police van had closed.

With Okoro's help and a letter in Vane's own hand, the true deed was placed in Imelda Crane's hands before the week was out, and the land beside the harbour returned to the fishing families who had lost it. Captain Frost was told that the old lifeboat house would be rebuilt on its original site, and he accepted the news with a gruff cough that could not quite hide a tear. Vane's last wish, it seemed, had been carried out, though not in the way that he had planned.

By the following spring the harbour at Harrow Bay had changed, for Imelda Crane's café was crowded with fishermen at every hour, and the new lifeboat house rang its bell on the first fine morning in April. Felix Okoro, who now worked for an honest lawyer in town, called in each week for a bowl of her fish soup, and old Captain Frost sat in the window and told anyone who would listen about the storms of his youth. Even the Grand Harrow Hotel, under its new manager, was said to be kinder to its guests.

Before she left the station, Miss Birch pressed Ada's hand between her small, dry ones and declared that in forty years of teaching she had seldom met anyone with such a sharp mind and such a kind heart. The railway company, once it had read the inspector's report, offered Ada a desk and a better wage in the head office, but she thanked them politely and asked to keep her lamp and her ticket book. A guard, she explained, sees things that no one at a desk ever will.

When the little railway opened again in the spring, the first train of the year pulled out of Carlow Junction in warm sunshine, and Ada Penrose stood at the carriage door with her lamp, her ticket book and a peppermint in her pocket. She smiled at each passenger as they boarded, as she always did, and she noticed everything about them, as she always would. For there is no train, she had learned, so ordinary that it does not carry at least one secret to the end of the line.
